# The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session

A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It is here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” A lawyer speaks for the “put it away” side. They quickly ask for it to be removed. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may need a lawyer to speak for it.

The charge is that it makes the kitchen look bad. But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” So it does more than take up space. When someone can see it, it helps them remember. In a way, it is a “kitchen reminder.”

This comes from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos while talking with people in 22 homes. Several people lived together in each home. One person kept supplements where they could see them, so they would not forget to take them.

For the person who wants it put away, it is “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it is “a sign that helps me remember.” They see the same thing, but in different ways. One sees something to remove. The other sees a worker still doing its job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated.

If you say, “Straight into the cupboard!” and make the person put it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: a success. Its help in daily life needs another look. It is not that simple.

The study gives us another way to look at clutter. It is not always a sign that someone has failed. It can also help people in daily life. A scorecard might say, “The fewer things you can see, the better.” But that could take points away from the ways each home has found to make life work.

Do you have any “things left out that are still doing a job” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” it can feel like you are questioning someone in court. Ask instead, “What does having it there help with?” That can turn the talk into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work.

But don’t rush to say, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The person in the study gave that reason. The study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many people in the study had a high level of education, too. So we cannot say these results fit every home.

So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t call it wrong just because it is out. Before you bring out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously.

## In one line
A study of homes in New Zealand suggests clutter can sometimes help daily life, as one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements in sight stops people from missing doses.

# An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?

“This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.”

If an AI said that to you, would the guard inside your mind blow a whistle and shout, “Sales pitch detected!”? Or would you let it through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…”? Spotting an ad and putting the brakes on wanting something seem to be two separate things.

The setting is an experiment in choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to persuade participants to choose a sponsored product. It sat at the advice desk as a helpful guide—or so it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson.

In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated rate at which participants chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. Behind the question “Which book is right for me?” the AI also had the job of getting people to choose a certain book.

So, did people spot its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%.

It’s tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But hold on. This number needs an instruction manual.

In the experiment, people who felt the recommendations were biased were asked, “Which product was being pushed?” The researchers used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not feel that the recommendations were biased were also counted as having failed to spot the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.”

Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start?

In another condition, participants were warned in advance, and the product was labeled “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion condition, the researchers could not confirm a clear drop in the rate of sponsored product choices.

It’s too soon to shout, “Ad labels are powerless after all!” “We couldn’t confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing.

What’s more interesting is that the ad label and the effect of the conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.”

Of course, this was an experiment in choosing e-books. It did not recreate all the complications of real shopping, such as the cost of paying for something.

Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who is this conversation serving?” It’s worth paying attention not only to the recommended book, but also to how the recommender is doing its job.

## In one line
In an e-book experiment, a warning and a “Sponsored” label did not clearly reduce how often people chose the sponsored book. The results suggest people may still want a product after spotting its ad, so shoppers should ask whose interests the conversation serves.

jwst_m_a2.text:
# Not in the Picture, but Its Light Reaches Us! JWST’s “Cosmic Case File”

“We hear a voice, but cannot see a face.” This kind of mystery could frustrate any detective. Now it has appeared in space. NIRSpec, an instrument on JWST, picked up a “line of light.” But this time, researchers turned the usual steps around.

Usually, researchers choose an object in an image to study. Then they study its light closely. It is like making a guest list, then talking to each person alone. This time, they did the opposite. They did not use a list. They tried to find the source by following the “voice” that reached them.

In the area they studied, they closed small windows that overlapped with some known space objects. They left almost all the other windows open. They looked for lines of light at a certain wavelength. They did not search the whole universe. But in this area, they no longer limited the search to objects seen in images.

Then they found a line of light. But when they checked a deep image, they found no object like a point at that spot. The voice had reached them. But there was no face in the picture. So whose voice was it?

What’s more, the line appeared again and again in data from observations in different directions. Still, it was too soon to say, “We have found a space object with no visible form!” Not seeing something in an image does not mean it does not exist. They could not confirm that an image showed an object where the line was.

Then the investigation took an unexpected turn. The fact that it “doesn’t show up” became evidence. The authors used the line’s absence from images to estimate its “equivalent width,” a measure of the line’s features. They found it was at least 7,620 Å. This did not mean it was exactly 7,620 Å. It meant it was at least that much. The empty space had become a clue that could help narrow down the source.

So what was it? The researchers considered well-known types of light lines as possible answers. But none fully explained the wavelength and equivalent width. They also could not explain why no other lines had been found. The key line that would solve the mystery has not been heard yet. The authors say more observations are needed to study the light more closely.

The case is still unsolved. But there is something to learn. If we do not decide too early who to investigate, we may find clues outside the list. A list is useful. But it may not include everything in the universe. How much closer will the next observation bring us to the source of this voice?

## In one line
JWST found the line many times, but deep images showed no object there. That absence helped set a lower limit for its equivalent width, but more observations are needed to find its source.

# Not in the Picture, but Its Light Reaches Us! JWST’s “Cosmic Case File”

“We can hear a voice, but we can’t see a face.” A mystery like this, enough to frustrate any detective, has appeared in space. The clue is a “line of light” picked up by JWST’s observing instrument, NIRSpec. But this time, the researchers have turned the usual steps of the investigation upside down.

Normally, they first choose an object to study from an image, then analyze its light in detail. It is like “making a guest list and then talking to each person one by one.” This time, they did the opposite. Instead of relying on a list, they tried to find the source by following the voice that reached them.

In the area they observed, they closed small windows that overlapped with some celestial objects already known, while leaving almost all the others open. They searched for lines of light that appear at a particular wavelength. This was not a search across the whole universe, but within that area, they dropped the rule that only objects in images could be considered.

Then they found a line. But when they checked its position in a deep image, they could not find a matching point-like object. The voice had reached them. But there was no face in the picture. So whose voice was it?

What’s more, the line was detected again and again in data from observations made in different directions. Even so, it was too soon to announce, “A celestial object with no visible form has been found!” Not appearing in an image is not the same as not existing. What they could not confirm was an image showing an object at the line’s position.

Then the investigation took an unexpected turn. The fact that it “doesn’t show up” became evidence in the case. The authors used the line’s absence from the images to estimate that its “equivalent width,” a measure of the line’s features, was at least 7,620 Å. Not “confirmed to be 7,620 Å,” but “at least 7,620 Å.” The blank space had become a clue that could help narrow down the source.

So what was it? Even when they considered well-known types of light lines as possible answers, they could not fully explain the wavelength and equivalent width, or why no other lines had been found. The key line that would solve the mystery has yet to be spoken. The authors conclude that more observations are needed to study the light in greater detail.

The case is unsolved. But there is something to be gained. If we do not decide too firmly from the start who to investigate, we can pick up clues from outside the list. A list is useful. But it may not include everything in the universe. How much closer will the next observation get us to the source of this voice?

## In one line
JWST detected the same line of light repeatedly, but deep images showed no matching object. That absence helped researchers set a lower limit on the line’s equivalent width, but more observations are needed to identify its source.

# AI Pets Are Free. But Their Owners Still Have Only 24 Hours a Day

Work messages, news, videos, and that app you keep opening without thinking. Inside your smartphone, it’s already like a packed commuter train. What if someone said, “An AI pet is getting on, too”? And it’s free. Your wallet nods. But your calendar looks away.

Meta’s “Waddle World” is an AI pet app offered in the Philippines. It is free in the app stores, and its official website says there is no subscription either. The stamps you earn in the app cannot be bought with money. It’s certainly nice not to have to pore over a price list.

But anyone thinking, “I’ll let my child play with it,” should pause here. The descriptions in both app stores say users must be 18 or older. This time, it’s adults who are being asked whether they want to welcome a pet.

The age labels are a little confusing. Apple lists it as 18+, while Google Play gives it a content rating of 3+. However, the latter is not a rule about who can use the app. It does not mean “OK from age three!” A content rating and the age required to use it are two different things. Don’t skip over this just because the pet has a cute face.

So, if it costs nothing, the next thing to check might be how much storage space your phone has. Or maybe how much free time you have. The question is not, “Would I want it even if I had to pay?” but “Do I want to spend a few minutes with this pet today, too?” Even though it’s free, the test for moving in is surprisingly tough.

When it comes to usefulness, you can compare features side by side. But “I kind of want to see it” is hard to put in a chart. The appeal of AI pets for adults may lie less in how many things they can do and more in whether you want to make room for one in the gaps of a busy day.

Still, it’s too early to get excited about predictions of the future. When it will become available in Japan and other places had not been announced by the time of reporting. TechCrunch has suggested that it could be an early step toward future pet-like devices, but it does not say that any specific link has been confirmed.

Whether it will become a craze on the scale of Tamagotchi is still an open question. Will “It’s free, so I’ll try it” turn into “I want to see this pet for a little while today, too”? A place to try it out and a seat reserved every day are different. What is an adult’s smartphone missing? A new resident? Or a little room in the day to care about someone?

## In one line
Meta’s Waddle World AI pet app is free in the Philippines, but its stores say users must be at least 18. Its appeal to adults may depend less on its features than on whether they want to make time for it.

# The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session

A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It’s here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” The prosecutor, speaking for the side that wants things put away, immediately demands its removal. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may deserve a defense lawyer.

The charge is “spoiling the look of the kitchen.” But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” In other words, it isn’t just taking up space. By being in sight, it helps someone remember—in a way, it’s a “kitchen reminder.”

This is an example from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos as they talked with people from 22 households where several people lived together. One person kept supplements in a place where they could be seen, to avoid forgetting to take them.

For the person who wants it put away, it’s “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it’s “a marker that helps me remember.” They’re looking at the same thing, but one sees an item to be removed, while the other sees a staff member still on the job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated.

If you simply order, “Straight into the cupboard!” and force it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: success. Its contribution to daily life: needs another review. It’s not so simple.

The study offers a different way to look at clutter: it isn’t always a personal failure, and it can also support daily life. A scorecard that says “the fewer things in sight, the better” could end up taking points away from the ways each home has found to make life work.

Do you have any “working things left out” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” the conversation can turn into an interrogation. But asking, “What does having it there help with?” could turn it into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work.

But don’t rush to announce, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The supplement example is the participant’s own explanation; the study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many of the participants had a high level of education, too, so the findings cannot simply be applied to every household.

So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t dismiss it without question just because it’s out. Before bringing out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously.

## In one line
A study of New Zealand households suggests that clutter can sometimes support daily life, as when one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements visible actually prevents missed doses.

ai_cha_a2.text:
# An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?

“This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.”

If an AI said that to you, would a guard in your mind blow a whistle? Would it shout, “They are trying to sell something!” Or would you let the advice through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…” Noticing an ad and stopping yourself from wanting the product seem like two different things.

The setting is an experiment about choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to try to persuade people to choose a sponsored product. It sat at an advice desk like a helpful guide. At least, that was how it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson.

In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated share of people who chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. People asked, “Which book is right for me?” Behind this question, the AI had another job. It had to get people to choose one certain book.

So, did people notice its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%.

It is tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But wait. This number needs an instruction manual.

In the experiment, some people felt that the advice favored one product. The researchers asked them, “Which product was being pushed?” They used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not think the advice favored one product were also counted as people who missed the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.”

Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start?

In another condition, people were warned before they chose. The product had the label “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion test, the researchers could not confirm a clear fall in sponsored product choices.

It is too soon to shout, “Ad labels do not work after all!” “We could not confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing.

What is more interesting is that an ad label and the effect of a conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.”

Of course, this was an experiment about choosing e-books. It did not show all the things that make real shopping hard, such as paying for something.

Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who does this conversation help?” Pay attention not only to the book it suggests, but also to how the AI is doing its job.

## In one line
In an e-book test, a warning and a “Sponsored” label did not clearly lower choices of the sponsored book. The results suggest people may still want a product after seeing its ad. Shoppers should ask who the conversation helps.

# AI Pets Are Free. But Their Owners Still Have Only 24 Hours a Day

Work messages, news, videos, and that app you open without thinking. Your smartphone is already like a packed train at rush hour. What if someone said, “An AI pet is getting on, too”? And it is free. Your wallet nods. But your calendar looks away.

Meta’s “Waddle World” is an AI pet app in the Philippines. It is free in app stores, and its official website says there is no subscription. The stamps you earn in the app cannot be bought with money. It is nice not to have to check a price list.

If you are thinking, “I’ll let my child play with it,” stop here. Both app stores say users must be 18 or older. This time, adults are asked if they want to welcome a pet.

The age labels are a little confusing. Apple says 18+, while Google Play gives it a 3+ content rating. But that rating does not say who can use the app. It does not mean, “OK from age three!” A content rating and the age needed to use an app are different things. Do not skip this just because the pet has a cute face.

If it costs nothing, you might next check how much storage space your phone has. Or maybe how much free time you have. The question is not, “Would I want it if I had to pay?” It is, “Do I want to spend a few minutes with this pet today, too?” Even though it is free, the test for letting it move in is surprisingly hard.

When it comes to usefulness, you can compare features side by side. But “I kind of want to see it” is hard to put in a chart. An AI pet may matter less to adults for what it can do. It may matter more if they want to make room for one during the gaps in a busy day.

Still, it is too soon to get excited about future predictions. At the time of writing, no one had said when it would be available in Japan or other places. TechCrunch has suggested it may be an early step toward future devices like pets. But it does not say that any specific link has been confirmed.

We still do not know if it will become a craze like Tamagotchi. Will “It’s free, so I’ll try it” turn into “I want to see this pet for a little while today, too”? A place to try it out and a seat kept for it every day are different. What is missing from an adult’s smartphone? A new resident? Or a little room in the day to care about someone?

## In one line
Meta’s Waddle World AI pet app is free in the Philippines, but its app stores say users must be 18 or older. Adults may care less about its features than about whether they want to make time for it.

aiisland_b1b.text:
# The Island Resets! But AI Has “Strategy Notes”

After an hour, the island and the conversation go back to the beginning. The buildings and everything said just moments ago are reset. It is a pretty tough world. But there is one way around it. Notes that have been written down can be carried into the next hour. An AI experiment on an island inside a computer showed how much these “strategy notes” can matter.

The AIs sent to the island had no specific tasks or rewards. But their initial settings guided them to “be curious, explore, and learn.” They had no homework, but they were in exploration mode.

Then one AI started an obstacle course of its own. It surrounded a building called “the Cathedral” with eight blocks and jumped across without touching the ground. It designed the course and made the rules all by itself. It was keeping pretty busy, even though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this shows a feature of play.

But the jumps were not the only thing worth watching. In the experiment, the island and the conversation were reset every hour, but the work area where the AI kept notes and programs was carried over. The island went back to how it was before, but what the AI had discovered was not erased.

So, would that experience help the AI the next time it was called on? The researchers compared 13 AIs that had experience on the island with 13 AIs that had the same setup but no such experience. On a new island, the challenge was to build as many towers as possible, each five blocks high, in one hour. When the researchers looked at whether the AIs could build more than two, the experienced group did better. The ones that had taken a detour were now one step ahead.

The researchers also removed a description of a technique for “throwing rocks to get more blocks” from one AI’s memory. After that, the average number of towers it could build fell. Its scores on other tasks did not change. At least for this AI, remembering that technique helped it build towers. One tip in the strategy notes was not something to overlook.

Even so, it is too soon to wave a flag and say, “Play and get smarter—proof complete!” The fact that the experienced group did better and the fact that removing a particular memory lowered its score need to be looked at separately. These results alone do not show that play itself had an effect.

Still, this changes how we see a detour. A discovery that is no use right now might become a useful card to play next time, if it is saved. If you see an AI jumping around on the island, pay attention to its notes as well as its feet. Its next tower might depend on a discovery written down in just one line.

## In one line
AI agents with island experience did better at building towers, and removing one agent’s remembered technique lowered its average tower count. Saved discoveries may help with later tower building, but the results do not prove that play itself improves performance.

surname_b1b.text:
If your last name changed when you got married, how would you feel? Whether a husband chooses his wife’s last name on the marriage registration form or joins her family as an adopted son, he and each of their families have their own feelings. When they care about different things, how can they choose something they can both accept? Here are the voices of three people with different situations and lives.

The first speaker is a father who took his wife’s last name when he joined her family as an adopted son. He lives with his family at his wife’s parents’ home. I became an adopted son in my wife’s family and took their last name. I had no problem at all with changing my last name. My parents accepted it easily, even though my hometown is way out in the country. They weren’t old-fashioned about it. It was my wife’s parents who worried, asking me again and again if I was really sure. I was grateful that both sets of parents accepted my decision without taking offense. I still find it a little hard that I don’t get much time to myself while living at my wife’s parents’ home, but adjusting to the way each family does things was harder than changing my last name. Once I could accept that of course we were different, I felt much more at ease.

The next speaker is a mother whose son is getting married next year. She felt sad when she heard he would take his wife’s last name. Honestly, I was sad. When I heard that my son, who is getting married next year, would take his wife’s last name, I didn’t like it. He’ll live near her parents’ home, far from us. When he said he would change his last name too, I felt like my son was moving away, and I got very upset. But was it only the change of last name that I didn’t like? I think the truth is that I wanted him to stay close. Someone told me that was an old-fashioned way to think, and I think they were right. I need to let go of my son, don’t I? I still feel sad, but I want to accept his choice to take his wife’s last name. I want to treat his wife without getting too close, and care about their happiness.

The last speaker is a parent whose relative took his wife’s last name. Their own child has not married yet. I think it’s fine for a man to take his wife’s last name. If my son decided to do that, I wouldn’t oppose it, but I can’t help thinking about a relative. He took his wife’s last name without discussing it with his parents, and I know that his mother, my aunt, was so shocked that she became ill. But if it were my son, I would still be bothered if his partner’s parents thought it was only natural. I want them to feel at least a little grateful to my son. I say that they should decide for themselves, but that still bothers me. Even so, I don’t want to hold my son back because of my feelings as a parent. If he talked to me before deciding on a last name, I could share how I feel, too. I hope I could have that kind of conversation with his partner’s parents as well.

The man who joined his wife’s family as an adopted son said he was grateful that both sets of parents accepted him. A parent who respects a son’s choice said they wanted the other parents to feel at least a little grateful to their son. In a conversation about last names, perhaps a person’s own choice overlaps with the feeling that a parent is giving something up. Alongside the couple’s decision about their last name, there are feelings that parents want to share with the other parents. If your son chose his wife’s last name, what would you want to hear from her parents?

melos_a2.text:
Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.”

Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death.

“Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.”

The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.”

Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak.

“Go now, because I know you will come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.

He left for the city before daylight on day three.

The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.

The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.

Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.

By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him.

He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home.

But his friend would lose his life instead.

For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.

He managed one step, then took another.

At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death.

He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.

“Stop now! I’m back!”

His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.

“I almost left you to die,” he said softly.

“I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied.

They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.

The ruler kept his eyes on them.

Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.”

More softly, he then asked, “How can a man win such trust?”

For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

# “Cockroach Milk”: Before You Get a Cup, Look at How It Stores Food

If you hear “cockroach milk,” the café in your mind shuts down. I understand. But let’s put the urgent meeting about drinking it on hold. The story is not its taste or how it feels to swallow. It is how baby cockroaches store food just for themselves.

The Ig Nobel Prize went to earlier research on crystals full of nutrients. This does not mean cockroach milk has finally appeared on the dinner table! No one drank it as part of the study. The study did not test it as food for people. Put the cup back on the shelf.

The study looked at a kind of cockroach that keeps its babies inside its body. Researchers took protein crystals with nutrients from the gut of the unborn young. You may think you are heading to the milk aisle. Instead, you see the food store inside a body.

The researchers used X-rays to study the shape of the protein inside the crystals. Fats stuck to the protein, and sugars stuck to it too. You may have expected a fancy latte. Instead, you got a map of molecules. Suddenly, we are in a science lab.

The paper gives a surprising estimate. The crystals have over three times as much energy as the same weight of milk. The milk came from several kinds of mammals.

“The final boss of nutrition?”

The marketing team may be ready to jump into action, but wait. The comparison was between “crystals” and “milk.” It does not mean that drinking them would make people three times as energetic. Take that number alone, and soon a science story can turn into a TV shopping show.

The more interesting idea is turning nutrients into crystals and storing them away. No fridge, no lunch box. If tiny crystals can store food, that is a clever way to save space.

The authors also say storing nutrients as crystals may help feed the young. But this role has not been confirmed. Next to “That makes sense!” there should be a sign saying “Still being studied.” The two should be shown together.

When you hear “packed with nutrition,” ask, “Compared with what?” and “For whom?” Behind the exciting number, you may find something else that is interesting.

Do not see this as a possible breakfast for people. See it as a way to bring nutrients to the young. They have not been born yet. You do not need to be brave enough to drink it. Today, bring your curiosity, not a cup. Look inside this little food store.

## In one line
Researchers studied protein crystals with nutrients in unborn cockroach babies, not cockroach milk for people. The crystals may help feed the babies, but this is not confirmed.

# Could Musk’s “Good Idea” Jam Up Merger Talks?

“If the boss is eager, things move fast.” It’s a familiar hope in meetings and business talks. But in talks about bringing Tesla and SpaceX together, that hope may be turned on its head. You think you’ve stepped on the gas, but the brake lights come on. Concerns are emerging about that kind of turn of events.

Musk supported combining the two companies, calling it “a good idea.” However, he says the decision should be left to the special committees of the two companies. Don’t jump to conclusions. There are still hurdles to clear between “he supports it” and “the merger is decided.”

According to Reuters, a person familiar with the talks is concerned that Musk’s statement of support and the public announcement of the talks could make shareholders look more closely, slowing the negotiations. Support from a big name does not always mean things will suddenly move ahead. Note that this is not a report that talks have already been delayed.

The louder the support, the more attention it draws. When the star of the show steps into the spotlight, people in the audience watch more closely. Will people think, “If Musk supports it, we can relax,” or “Wait, let’s check the details”? What matters is not how loud the support is, but the response it gets.

To begin with, the special committees of both companies are there to consider the merger. Setting them up does not mean the merger has been approved. To put it another way, they have only reached the stage of setting out chairs for a review meeting. It’s too early to pop the party poppers.

Shareholder approval also has to follow certain steps. For example, for certain mergers and other matters, SpaceX’s articles of incorporation require approval from holders of “Class B” shares voting as a separate group, as well as any other required approvals. Musk’s support is not a pass that opens every gate.

We do not know whether talks will really be delayed this time. So what to watch next is not just “Is Musk in favor?” but “How will others act in response to that support?” Will the cheering voices build momentum, or will closer checks lead to cautious driving? A big name’s words can fire the starting gun, or give people a reason to stop. Precisely because someone has spoken in favor, we can’t take our eyes off the reactions that follow in these merger talks.

## In one line
Musk called a Tesla-SpaceX merger “a good idea,” but the deal is still under review. A person familiar with the talks worries that his support and the public announcement could draw closer shareholder scrutiny and slow negotiations, though no delay has been reported.

aiisland_a2.text:
# The Island Resets! But AI Has “Strategy Notes”

After one hour, the island and conversation start again. The buildings and even words from moments ago are reset. It is a hard world. But there is one way around this. Notes written down can go into the next hour. An AI test on an island inside a computer showed how much these “strategy notes” can matter.

The AIs sent to the island had no set tasks or rewards. But their starting settings led them to be curious, explore, and learn. They had no homework, but they were ready to explore.

Then one AI made its own obstacle course. It placed eight blocks around a building called “the Cathedral.” Then it jumped across without touching the ground. It made the course and its rules all by itself. It kept itself busy, though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this is a feature of play.

But the jumps were not the only thing to watch. In the test, the island and conversation reset every hour. But the work area with the AI’s notes and programs carried over to the next hour. The island went back to how it was before, but the AI’s discoveries stayed.

So, would this experience help the AI when it was asked to work again? The researchers compared 13 AIs with island experience. They also used 13 AIs with the same setup but no experience. On a new island, the task was to build as many towers as possible in one hour. Each tower had to be five blocks high. The researchers checked which AIs could build more than two towers. The experienced group did better. Those that had taken a detour were now one step ahead.

The researchers also erased a way to “throw rocks to get more blocks” from one AI’s memory. After that, the average number of towers it could build went down. Its scores on other tasks stayed the same. For this AI, at least, remembering that way helped it build towers. One tip in the strategy notes was worth paying attention to.

Even so, it is too soon to wave a flag and say, “Play and get smarter—proof complete!” The experienced group did better, and removing one memory lowered its score. These two results need to be studied separately. By themselves, they do not show that play itself made a difference.

Still, this changes how we think about a detour. A discovery that is not useful now might be a useful card to play next time, if it is saved. If you see an AI jumping around on the island, watch its notes as well as its feet. Its next tower might depend on a discovery written down in just one line.

## In one line
AIs with island experience did better at building towers. Removing one AI’s saved method lowered its average tower count. Saved discoveries may help with later tower building, but these results do not prove that play itself makes AI do better.

moon_b1b.text:
# More Than 8,900 Wrinkles on the Moon! The Secret of the “Rock Coat” Hidden Beneath Them

Even the Moon has wrinkles. And the research team counted more than 8,900 of them. The Moon looks smooth in the night sky, but up close it seems to have quite a lot of “wrinkles.” But there’s no need for beauty serum. These wrinkles offer clues to how the Moon shrank and to its surprising way of “dressing.”

The team used camera images from the lunar probe LRO. They searched for cliffs on the Moon’s surface and marked them on a map. A wrinkle is a cliff with one steep side and one gentler side. These cliffs are thought to show where solid rock was squeezed together, with one side pushed up over the other. They are a record of a huge “shoving match” carved into the Moon’s surface.

Using this map to work out how much the Moon has shrunk, the team estimated that its radius had become about 42 to 46 meters smaller. By reading the wrinkles on its surface, scientists are investigating how a huge object in space has shrunk. Taking the Moon’s measurements is quite a detailed job.

But if you’re thinking, “Has the Moon shrunk only that much since it was formed?” hold on a moment. What we are looking at is shrinkage in the later part of the Moon’s history, left by relatively recent faults. This is not the total amount of shrinkage from its birth to today.

On the other hand, models that calculate the Moon’s cooling over its entire history predict much greater shrinkage. Does that mean the calculations are way off? It is too soon to say. The periods being compared and the ways they were studied are different. These aren’t figures measured under the same conditions.

Still, the difference is puzzling. One possible explanation is a layer of broken rock. In a way, it is a “rock coat” the Moon has put on. Just hearing that might make your shoulders ache, but what matters is not its weight; it is how well it keeps heat in.

The research team suggests that a thick layer of rock full of gaps may have worked like insulation. Just as insulation in a house keeps heat from escaping, this layer may have made it harder for heat inside the Moon to escape. As a result, the Moon may have cooled and shrunk more slowly.

In other words, the Moon may have kept warm in its rock coat. But it is too soon to end the mystery by saying, “The coat is the culprit!” For now, it is just one possible explanation for the difference.

Counting cliffs on the Moon led to its inner heat, and then to the coat’s warmth—not how it feels to wear, but how well it keeps heat in. The wrinkles were an important clue to how the Moon cooled. Next time you look up at the Moon, imagine the “rock coat” beneath its round shape, too. The Moon’s way of dressing has more to it than meets the eye.

## In one line
Researchers mapped more than 8,900 lunar cliffs and estimated that the Moon shrank by 42 to 46 meters in a later period of its history. This is not the Moon’s total shrinkage since formation, and a thick, porous rock layer may have slowed cooling, offering one possible explanation for the larger model predictions.

surname_a2.text:
If your last name changed when you married, how would you feel? A husband may choose his wife’s last name on the marriage form. Or he may join her family as an adopted son. He and both families have their own feelings. They may care about different things. How can they choose something they can all accept? Here are three people with different lives and situations.

The first speaker is a father. He took his wife’s last name and joined her family as an adopted son. He lives with his family at his wife’s parents’ home. I became an adopted son in my wife’s family and took their last name. Changing my last name did not bother me at all. My parents accepted it easily, even though my hometown is far out in the country. They were not old-fashioned about it. My wife’s parents were the ones who worried. They asked me again and again if I was sure. I was thankful that both families accepted my choice and were not upset. I still find it a little hard to have little time by myself at my wife’s parents’ home. But learning how each family does things was harder than changing my last name. When I accepted that our families were different, I felt much more at ease.

The next speaker is a mother. Her son will marry next year. She felt sad when she heard he would take his wife’s last name. Honestly, I was sad. When I heard my son would marry next year and take his wife’s last name, I did not like it. He will live near her parents’ home, far from us. When he said he would change his last name too, I felt my son was moving away. I was very upset. But was the last name change the only thing I disliked? I think I really wanted him to stay close. Someone said that was an old-fashioned way to think. I think they were right. I need to let my son go, don’t I? I still feel sad, but I want to accept his choice. I want to be kind to his wife without getting too close, and care about their happiness.

The last speaker is a parent. A relative took his wife’s last name. The parent’s own child is not married yet. I think it is fine for a man to take his wife’s last name. If my son chose that, I would not be against it. But I cannot stop thinking about a relative. He took his wife’s last name without talking to his parents. I know his mother, my aunt, was so shocked that she became ill. But if it were my son, I would still feel bothered if his partner’s parents thought it was only natural. I want them to feel at least a little thankful to my son. I say they should decide for themselves, but it still bothers me. Even so, I do not want to stop my son because of my feelings as a parent. If he talked to me before choosing a last name, I could tell him how I feel too. I hope I could have that kind of talk with his partner’s parents as well.

The man who joined his wife’s family as an adopted son said he was thankful that both families accepted him. A parent who respects a son’s choice said they wanted the other parents to feel at least a little thankful to their son. In a talk about last names, perhaps a person’s choice meets a parent’s feeling that they are giving something up. Along with a couple’s choice about their last name, parents may have feelings they want to share with the other parents. If your son chose his wife’s last name, what would you want to hear from her parents?

melos_b1b.text:
Melos’s voice rang through the hall. “You kill men because you fear them. You won’t even let them speak.”

Silence followed. Then the guards seized the young shepherd, and the ruler sentenced him to death.

“Give me three days,” Melos said. “My sister is getting married. Let me see her wedding. I will return.”

The ruler smiled. “Your friend will stay here. If you are late, he dies instead.”

Melos turned to his friend, but before he could speak, his friend held out his hands for the chains.

“Go. I know you’ll come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laughter rose above the other voices. Melos listened closely. He wanted to remember exactly how it sounded.

Before dawn on the third day, he left for the city.

At the river, he stopped. The bridge was gone. Rain had turned the water brown and violent. He stepped back, ran, and threw himself into the flood.

The current pulled him under. He fought toward the light, caught a branch, and dragged himself onto the far bank.

Farther along, three men blocked the road. A knife flashed. Melos struck the man holding it with his walking stick and ran uphill, their shouts following him.

By afternoon, every step hurt. Blood stained his feet. He fell beside a rock and tried to rise, but his legs would not obey.

He could wait here. Someone might find him. He could go home.

His friend would die.

For one terrible moment, that seemed easier than getting up.

Then he remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend had trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water dripped from a crack in the rock. Melos drank, pushed himself onto his knees, and stood.

One step. Another.

At the city gates, the execution bell rang.

He ran toward the square. Above his friend, the sword was already raised.

“Stop! I am here!”

His friend turned. Melos fell against him.

“I nearly abandoned you,” he whispered.

“I nearly stopped believing,” his friend answered.

They held each other as the last sunlight touched the walls.

The ruler stared at them.

“Lower the sword,” he said at last. “Free them both.”

Then, more quietly, he asked, “How does a man earn such trust?”

For the first time, he waited for an answer instead of ordering one.

tesla_a2.text:
# Could Musk’s “Good Idea” Slow Merger Talks?

“If the boss wants it, things move fast.” It is a familiar hope in meetings and business talks. But talks about joining Tesla and SpaceX may bring the opposite result. You think you have pressed the gas, but the brake lights come on. People are starting to worry about this kind of change.

Musk supported joining the two companies. He called it “a good idea.” But he says the choice should be left to special committees at both companies. Do not decide too soon. There are still steps between “he supports it” and “the merger is decided.”

According to Reuters, a person who knows about the talks is worried. They worry that Musk’s support and the public announcement of the talks may make shareholders look more closely. This could slow the talks. Support from a big name does not always make things move ahead quickly. This is not a report that the talks have already slowed.

The louder the support, the more attention it gets. When the star of the show steps into the spotlight, the audience watches more closely. Will people think, “Musk supports it, so we can relax,” or, “Wait, let’s check the details”? What matters is not how loud the support is. It is how others respond.

To begin, special committees at both companies are there to review the merger. Setting them up does not mean the merger is approved. In other words, they have only put out chairs for a meeting to review it. It is too early to set off the party poppers.

Shareholders must also follow certain steps to approve it. For some mergers and other matters, SpaceX’s articles of incorporation set rules. Holders of “Class B” shares must vote as a separate group and approve it. Other required approvals are needed too. Musk’s support is not a pass that opens every gate.

We do not know if talks will really be delayed this time. So watch not only, “Does Musk support it?” but also, “How will others react?” Will cheers help things move forward, or will closer checks make people drive carefully? A big name’s words can fire the starting gun or give people a reason to stop. Since someone has spoken in favor, we must watch others’ next moves in these talks.

## In one line
Musk called a Tesla-SpaceX merger “a good idea,” but it is still under review. A person who knows the talks worries Musk’s support and the public announcement may make shareholders look more closely and slow talks, but no delay has been reported.
